title: Why a written code
hookLine: a shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike

lines: A STRANGER IN A NEW CITY.
SHE ALREADY KNOWS WHAT TO DO.
cards: A woman lands in a city she has never seen, tired, far from her family. She finds a gurdwara on a side street and doesn't know a single person inside. But at the door she already knows what to do.
Shoes off. Head covered. Into the hall, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, sit with the sangat.
Later, down to the langar, where she sits on the floor in a row with strangers and is fed. Nobody had to explain any of it. How does that happen, and why did Sikhs bother to write it down?

teach.h: A PAGE CAN CROSS AN OCEAN.
teach.b: Four reasons. First, a written code travels. Spoken custom stays close to the village it grew in.
A page can cross an ocean, be read in a new language, be taught in a basement class in a city the Gurus never saw.

So Sikh families in two countries can open the same pages and find the same daily prayers, the same order for a wedding, the same form for the Ardas. One code, many homes. Second, it settles things more fairly.

teach.h: POINT TO A PAGE, NOT A VOICE.
teach.b: When two people disagree about how something should be done, they can point to a page instead of to whoever speaks loudest or has the most money. A rule on paper applies to the powerful and the poor alike.

Third, it gives the newcomer a starting place. Someone learning the path, or coming back after years away, can read what is asked instead of guessing or feeling foolish. Fourth, it keeps the community in conversation.
The shared code was agreed by Sikhs working together, and the Guru Panth can still discuss it. A written code doesn't replace the Guru, or love, or seva, or the remembrance of the Name.

teach.h: A COMMON DOORWAY, NOT THE GURU.
teach.b: It's more like a common doorway.
Families still bring their own warmth, their own food, their own way of laughing in the langar line. But the doorway is the same width wherever you find it, and anyone can walk through.

how: Gurdwaras in different countries follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada for daily prayers, ceremonies and conduct, so a Sikh visiting a gurdwara far from home recognizes the order of things.

games.q: what does “why a written code” mean?
o: so the code could stand in place of the Guru Granth
because spoken custom was banned by the old rulers
so Sikhs everywhere can share one way of doing things

games.q: why write it down: tap the pairs.
p: a page can cross an ocean
point to a page, not a voice

s: a written code replaces the Guru
the code is a common doorway. it doesn't replace the Guru, seva or remembrance of the Name.
a written rule applies to the powerful as well as the poor
that's one reason a page settles things more fairly than the loudest voice.
a shared code means every family's home life looks the same
families still bring their own warmth, food and ways. the doorway is shared.

games.q: two members of a gurdwara committee disagree on how a ceremony should go. what does a written code let them do?
o: point to the same page and read it together.
games.why: a written code lets people point to a page instead of a voice, so a rule applies the same way to everyone.

practice: Choose one rule your household keeps that nobody ever wrote down: shoes at the door, who sits where, what gets said before a meal.
Put it into one plain sentence, the way it would read for someone who just moved in, on paper or silently. Then sit with it and ask whether the sentence holds everything the habit does.

wordCard.voice: Why a written code. A shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one code, many homes. A page can travel where a village custom can't. Rest well.
